warmup.q: Redis holds no copy of shop m-17's name. Program A asks Redis, finds nothing, reads Fietsen Utrecht from the database, and then stops for 40 ms before it stores that name in Redis for an hour. During those 40 ms, program B saves the new name, Velo Utrecht, in the database and then deletes the shop's entry from Redis. What do customers see for the next hour?
options: Velo Utrecht: B deleted the entry after saving, so the next reader loads the new name
Fietsen Utrecht: A's store lands after B's delete and puts the old name back
No name from Redis at all: Redis refuses to store a key that was deleted a moment ago
Velo Utrecht, about 40 ms later: Redis notices that the two programs disagree and drops the entry
warmup.why: B's delete ran while Redis held nothing for the shop, so it deleted nothing. A's store arrives after it, carrying the name A read before B saved. No later save is coming to delete it, so every customer gets the old name until the hour runs out. Redis keeps no memory of a deleted key and knows nothing about what the database holds, so it can't notice anything. This lesson calls the race a stale set, and shows two ways to make Redis refuse that late store.

sections.h: Updating the cached copy on every save, and why deleting it is safer
sections.html:
Let's set up the app first. A small company runs the program that records card payments for shops. Each shop's details live in the database, the program that keeps the company's records on disk and has the final word on them. They sit in a table called merchants, because the code calls a shop a merchant, with one row per shop.

Reading the database for every payment is slow, so the app keeps copies in Redis, in memory, where reading is fast. Each copy is stored under a name, its key, here merchant:{m-17}. (The curly braces matter only when Redis runs on several machines, which Redis Cluster and production operations covers.)

The last lesson, Caching patterns and stampedes, gave the app two habits. On a read, ask Redis first, with GET. If nothing is there, which is called a miss, read the row from the database and store a copy with SET merchant:{m-17} "Fietsen Utrecht" EX 3600. EX 3600 gives the copy a TTL (time to live) of 3,600 seconds: after an hour, Redis deletes it by itself. On a save, commit the change to the database, which makes it permanent, and then delete the copy with DEL.

Fietsen Utrecht in Redis is a copy of one version of the row, as it was when some program read it. Every save makes a new version in the database, and the copy doesn't say which version it came from. That gives us this lesson's idea: a cache is honest as long as no copy older than the newest delete can get into it. Each race below is a way for an old copy to sneak in, and each fix is a way for Redis to refuse it.

Why delete at all, instead of writing the new name into Redis on every save? The company runs its program on several computers at once, called servers. Say two people edit the shop's name at almost the same moment. Writer A, on one server, saves Fietsen Utrecht. Writer B, on another, saves Velo Utrecht a moment later. Each commits, then sends SET with its new name.

The database ends with B's name, because B committed last. But each SET travels from its own server over its own network connection, and nothing puts them in the order of the commits. If A's server stalls for 20 ms, its SET arrives second. Redis keeps A's name, the database keeps B's, and nobody sees an error. The book Designing Data-Intensive Applications calls this a dual write: one change written separately to two systems, with nothing keeping them in step.

A delete fixes this case because it carries no value. Two deletes in either order leave the same empty key, and the next reader loads whatever the database committed last. Meta, the company behind Facebook, gives the same reason in its paper about memcache, its huge cache built from a program much like Redis. A delete is idempotent: it has the same effect however many times you repeat it, in any order.

Deleting closes this way in, but two more remain: a slow reader, and a server that crashes before its delete. The slow reader comes next.

try.title: Two updates that arrive out of order, then two deletes
steps: Start Redis from the labs folder if it isn't running (docker compose -f env/redis.yml up -d), and open its prompt: docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli. Docker runs Redis in a container, a sealed-off box on your laptop, and redis-cli is the program you type Redis commands into.
The first two lines are writer B's SET (B committed last) and writer A's SET, which arrived later because A's server stalled. Run them and the GET. Which writer's name does every reader get now?
Now replay the same two writers with deletes. Predict what the last GET prints, then run the last three lines.

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt

try.expect: The two SETs print OK and OK, and GET prints "Fietsen Utrecht": writer A's name, although writer B committed last. Redis keeps whatever arrived last, and nothing in it knows the order of the commits. With deletes, the first DEL prints (integer) 1, the second prints (integer) 0 (there was nothing left to delete), and GET prints (nil), Redis's word for nothing. The next reader goes to the database and caches the name committed last, whichever delete arrived first.

sections.h: The stale set: a slow reader puts the old name back after the delete
sections.html:
Deleting on every save leaves one race on the read side, and it takes three players. Reader A, a server checking a payment, misses on merchant:{m-17} and reads the row from the database: version 1, Fietsen Utrecht. Before A's SET reaches Redis, the writer commits version 2, Velo Utrecht, and sends DEL merchant:{m-17}. Redis holds nothing for the key yet, so the delete removes nothing.

Then A's SET arrives and stores version 1, with an hour of TTL. Reader B and every later reader get Fietsen Utrecht. Nothing will delete the key again, because the save that should have deleted it is already over. The stepper below plays it one step at a time.

Picture a shop window. The prices live on a list in the back office, and clerks copy them onto tags for the window. When a price changes, someone takes the old tag down, and the next clerk copies a fresh one. Now picture a slow clerk who copies the old price, stops for a coffee, and pins his tag up after the window was cleared. The list is the database, the window is Redis, and the slow clerk is reader A.

Storing a copy after a miss is called filling the cache, and the store is a fill. Meta's memcache paper calls this race a stale set: a fill that stores a value which was already out of date when it arrived.

Two things must both happen: A's read comes before the commit, and A's fill comes after the delete. Between a read and its fill there's usually a millisecond or two, but plenty of things stretch that gap to hundreds. Java, for example, stops a program for a moment now and then to clean up memory it no longer uses, a garbage-collection pause. A wait for a free connection to the database does the same. One save that lands inside the gap is enough.

So the race is rare for one request and frequent across millions. In 2022, Meta described it in TAO, the cache in front of its social-network data, which serves more than a quadrillion (a million billion) reads a day. A reader started to fill the cache with x = 42. Then x changed to 43, and a message about the change put 43 into the cache. The late fill then wrote 42 over it, and the cache said 42 for good. When Meta started measuring, about one cache write in a million was still wrong five minutes later: at that volume, a steady stream of wrong answers.

Here the TTL caps the damage at an hour. For a shop's name on a receipt, that's a nuisance. Now put a flag on the same row that says a shop is suspended, blocked from taking payments because of fraud. An hour of the old flag is an hour of payments that should have been refused.

The lab doesn't wait for a lucky pause. Each cache runs a hook, a small piece of code, between its database read and its fill. Two latches hold reader A in that hook until the writer has finished. A latch (Java's CountDownLatch) is a gate: one thread, a single line of work inside a program, waits at it until another thread opens it. With latches deciding the order, twenty runs give twenty stale caches.

To refuse A's late fill, Redis needs some way to tell that it's older than the delete. Next, we'll give it the first one: a ticket the delete can tear up.

try.title: Run the race four times, with four caches
steps: With Redis running, run StaleSetDemo (Java) or StaleSetDemoKt (Kotlin) from the labs folder. It plays the stepper's timeline four times, with latches, so the order is the same on every run: the last lesson's cache, a lease, a version check with a plain DEL, and a version check with a tombstone.

Before you read the output, predict for each race whether reader B gets Fietsen Utrecht (stale) or Velo Utrecht (fresh). The next two sections explain races 2 to 4. For now, look at what each one does differently on the W (writer) lines.
Read race 1 against the stepper: which output line is frame 4, and which is frame 5?

code.title: StaleSetDemo.java
code.html: package sfz.cache.l07.demo; import redis.clients.jedis.RedisClient; import redis.clients.jedis.params.SetParams; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** The stale-set race four times, always in the same order: reader A misses, the writer commits, A fills, B reads. */ public class StaleSetDemo { record Row(String name, long version) {} static final Map<String, Row> table = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); // the "database" static final RedisClient redis = RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build(); static final String KEY = "demo:l07:merchant:{m-17}"; static final String LEASE = "demo:l07:lease:{m-17}"; /** What a pod does on a read, and what the writer does after its commit. */ interface Cache { String get(String who, Runnable beforeFill); void afterWrite(long newVersion); } static void say(String who, String what) { System.out.printf(" %s %s%n", who, what); } // 1. lesson 6's cache-aside: GET, on a miss SELECT and SET; after a write, DEL static final Cache NAIVE = new Cache() { public String get(String who, Runnable beforeFill) { String hit = redis.get(KEY); if (hit != null) return hit; Row row = table.get("m-17"); say(who, "GET: miss. SELECT: " + row.name() + " (v" + row.version() + ")"); beforeFill.run(); redis.set(KEY, row.name(), SetParams.setParams().ex(3_600)); say(who, "SET " + row.name() + " EX 3600: OK"); return row.name(); } public void afterWrite(long v) { say("W", "DEL: " + redis.del(KEY) + " keys deleted"); } }; // 2. a lease: only the reader whose token is still in the lease key may fill static final String FILL_WITH_LEASE = """ if redis.call('GET', KEYS[2]) ~= ARGV[1] then return 0 end redis.call('SET', KEYS[1], ARGV[2], 'EX', 3600) redis.call('DEL', KEYS[2]) return 1 """; static final Cache LEASED = new Cache() { public String get(String who, Runnable beforeFill) { String hit = redis.get(KEY); if (hit != null) return hit; String token = "t-" + who; // readable; real code uses a UUID String took = redis.set(LEASE, token, SetParams.setParams().nx().px(10_000)); Row row = table.get("m-17"); say(who, "GET: miss. SET lease " + token + " NX PX 10000: " + took + ". SELECT: " + row.name() + " (v" + row.version() + ")"); beforeFill.run(); Object ok = redis.eval(FILL_WITH_LEASE, List.of(KEY, LEASE), List.of(token, row.name())); say(who, "fill with lease " + token + ": " + (Long.valueOf(1).equals(ok) ? "stored" : "refused, the lease is gone")); return row.name(); } public void afterWrite(long v) { say("W", "DEL value and lease: " + redis.del(KEY, LEASE) + " keys deleted"); } }; // 3 and 4. a version check: the entry is a hash {ver, name}; a fill older than what the cache has seen is refused static final String FILL_IF_NEWER = """ local seen = tonumber(redis.call('HGET', KEYS[1], 'ver')) if seen and seen > tonumber(ARGV[1]) then return 0 end redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'ver', ARGV[1], 'name', ARGV[2]) redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], 3600) return 1 """; static final String TOMBSTONE = """ local seen = tonumber(redis.call('HGET', KEYS[1], 'ver')) if seen and seen > tonumber(ARGV[1]) then return 0 end redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1]) redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'ver', ARGV[1]) redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[2]) return 1 """; static Cache versioned(boolean tombstone) { return new Cache() { public String get(String who, Runnable beforeFill) { String hit = redis.hget(KEY, "name"); // a tombstone has no name: a miss if (hit != null) return hit; Row row = table.get("m-17"); say(who, "HGET: miss. SELECT: " + row.name() + " (v" + row.version() + ")"); beforeFill.run(); Object ok = redis.eval(FILL_IF_NEWER, List.of(KEY), List.of(String.valueOf(row.version()), row.name())); say(who, "fill v" + row.version() + " if newer: " + (Long.valueOf(1).equals(ok) ? "stored" : "refused, the cache has seen v" + redis.hget(KEY, "ver"))); return row.name(); } public void afterWrite(long v) { if (tombstone) { redis.eval(TOMBSTONE, List.of(KEY), List.of(String.valueOf(v), "10000")); say("W", "tombstone: ver " + v + ", no name, for 10 s"); } else { say("W", "DEL: " + redis.del(KEY) + " keys deleted"); } } }; } static void race(String title, Cache cache) throws Exception { redis.del(KEY, LEASE); table.put("m-17", new Row("Fietsen Utrecht", 1)); System.out.println(title); CountDownLatch atFill = new CountDownLatch(1); CountDownLatch writerDone = new CountDownLatch(1); // reader A misses, reads v1, and stops just before its fill until the writer is done CompletableFuture<String> readerA = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> cache.get("A", () -> { atFill.countDown(); await(writerDone); })); await(atFill); table.put("m-17", new Row("Velo Utrecht", 2)); say("W", "UPDATE: Velo Utrecht (v2). COMMIT"); cache.afterWrite(2); writerDone.countDown(); readerA.get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); String b = cache.get("B", () -> {}); String db = table.get("m-17").name(); System.out.println(" B reads: " + b + (b.equals(db) ? " (fresh)" : " (STALE: the database says " + db + ", and the entry lives " + redis.ttl(KEY) + " s more)")); System.out.println(); } static void await(CountDownLatch latch) { try { if (!latch.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) throw new IllegalStateException("timed out"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { throw new IllegalStateException(e); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { race("1. cache-aside, DEL after the commit", NAIVE); race("2. a lease that the DEL revokes", LEASED); race("3. a version check, DEL after the commit", versioned(false)); race("4. a version check, a tombstone after the commit", versioned(true)); System.out.println("cleaning up: " + redis.del(KEY, LEASE) + " keys deleted"); redis.close(); } }

try.expect: Race 1 ends with B reads: Fietsen Utrecht (STALE: the database says Velo Utrecht, and the entry lives 3600 s more). Its W DEL: 0 keys deleted line is frame 4, and A SET Fietsen Utrecht EX 3600: OK is frame 5. In race 2, A's fill prints refused, the lease is gone, because the writer's DEL value and lease: 1 keys deleted removed A's token. B takes lease t-B, reads version 2 and gets Velo Utrecht (fresh). Race 3 is stale again: after a plain DEL, fill v1 if newer: stored, because the cache had no version left to compare with. Race 4 is fresh: the writer left tombstone: ver 2, so A's fill prints refused, the cache has seen v2, and B fills version 2. The Java and Kotlin demos print the same lines on every run, because latches decide the order. The last line is cleaning up: 1 keys deleted.

aside.title: Why not delete the key again, a moment later?
aside.html: Many blog posts suggest exactly that: delete the key, wait a few hundred milliseconds, and delete it once more to catch a late fill. It helps, because most slow readers finish within the wait. But it shrinks the gap without closing it, since a reader that pauses longer than the wait still gets in. And you have to guess how slow your slowest reader can be. The lease and the version in the next two sections close the gap without a guess.

video.title: How did the old name get back? The stale set and the lease

sections.h: A lease: a ticket that the delete can take away
sections.html:
The stale SET got in because deleting an empty key leaves no trace, so Redis had nothing left of the delete when the fill arrived. Let's give each miss something that the delete can take away.

Back to the shop window. Before a clerk copies a price, he takes a numbered ticket from the office. A price change tears up every ticket for that item, and the window accepts a tag only with a ticket that's still valid. The slow clerk comes back to find his ticket gone, and his old tag never goes up.

That ticket is a lease, the fix in Meta's memcache paper (Nishtala and others, 2013). On a miss, memcache hands the reader a token, a random number 64 bits long, tied to that key. To fill the key, the reader must show the token, and a delete of the key cancels it. So a fill that started before the save is refused.

Redis has no lease command, but it has the parts. On a miss, the reader takes the lease with SET lease:{m-17} <random token> NX PX 10000. NX (not exists) stores the value only if the key doesn't exist yet, so exactly one reader gets the lease. PX 10000 is a TTL of 10,000 milliseconds, so a crashed reader's lease vanishes after 10 seconds. After its commit, the writer deletes the copy and the lease in one command, DEL merchant:{m-17} lease:{m-17}. To fill, the reader checks that the lease still holds its token, then sets the value.

Those two steps can't have a gap between them, or a delete could land between the check and the SET. So the fill runs as a script. EVAL sends Redis a small program in Lua, a little programming language that Redis can run inside itself. Redis runs commands one at a time on a single thread (Inside an in-memory store: how Redis executes commands). It runs a whole script as one command, so no other program's command lands between its lines. Serial execution: Redis MULTI, WATCH and Lua covers scripts in full. This one needs four lines:

if redis.call('GET', KEYS[2]) ~= ARGV[1] then return 0 end   -- revoked by a write, or someone else's
redis.call('SET', KEYS[1], ARGV[2], 'EX', ARGV[3])
redis.call('DEL', KEYS[2])                                    -- done: the next miss may take a new lease
return 1

KEYS holds the key names the caller passes in and ARGV the other values, both counted from 1. Here KEYS[1] is the copy, KEYS[2] the lease, ARGV[1] the reader's token, ARGV[2] the name and ARGV[3] the TTL. In Lua, ~= means "not equal". If the lease holds someone else's token, or nothing, the script returns 0 and stores nothing. Otherwise it stores the name and gives the lease back.

Let's replay the race. Reader A takes the lease and stalls. The writer's DEL removes the lease along with the empty copy. A's fill finds no token, returns 0 and changes nothing. Reader B misses, takes a new lease, reads version 2 and fills it.

Leases also fix the last lesson's stampede, where a hundred requests miss the same key at once and all ask the database. Only one reader per key holds the lease, and the others wait a few milliseconds for its value. Meta hands out one token per key every 10 seconds. On keys prone to stampedes, its peak database load over a measured week fell from 17,000 queries a second to 1,300. A reader that waits too long reads the database itself, but never fills without a lease.

A lease works when every fill starts with a miss. Some writes into the cache don't, so next we'll meet a fix that covers them too.

steps: At the redis-cli prompt, run the first three lines. The DEL clears an earlier run, reader A takes the lease with token t-A, and reader B tries for it with t-B.
The fourth line is the writer's DEL after its commit. Then reader A shows t-A to the fill script. Predict the script's reply and the GET after it.
Run the rest: reader B misses, takes a fresh lease and fills version 2. What's left of the lease afterwards?

try.expect: DEL prints (integer) 0 on a fresh server. Reader A's SET ... NX prints OK: it holds the lease. Reader B's prints (nil): the lease is taken, so B would wait. The writer's DEL prints (integer) 1, the lease (the copy was never there). A's EVAL prints (integer) 0, refused, and GET prints (nil): the old name never reached the cache. B's second try at the lease prints OK, its fill prints (integer) 1, GET prints "Velo Utrecht", and EXISTS lease:{m-17} prints (integer) 0: the fill gave the lease back.

sections.h: A version number refuses any copy older than one the cache has seen
sections.html:
A lease protects fills that start with a miss. Some writes into the cache don't. A writer might store the new value directly, as the first section tried, or a program might copy every change from the database into Redis, as the last section will. For those, compare versions instead of tokens.

The database can already put each row's changes in order, with a version column that goes up by one on every save, or the time of the last update. Store that version with the copy. Redis has a type that holds both, the hash: a small table of named fields under one key (Core data types and their encodings). The copy becomes merchant:{m-17} = {ver: 1, name: Fietsen Utrecht}. Then make every write into the cache conditional: store this only if the cache holds nothing newer.

local seen = tonumber(redis.call('HGET', KEYS[1], 'ver'))
if seen and seen > tonumber(ARGV[1]) then return 0 end        -- the cache has seen a newer version
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'ver', ARGV[1], 'name', ARGV[2])
redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], 3600)
return 1

HGET reads one field of a hash, and HSET writes fields. tonumber turns the stored text into a number, and seen is nil, Lua's word for nothing, when there's no entry yet. In the shop window, the version is the date printed on every tag, and the window refuses a tag older than the one it last took down.

With versions, updating the cache on every save is safe again. In the first section's race between two writers, writer A's late SET carries version 2, while the cache already holds B's version 3, so the script refuses it. Uber, the ride-hailing company, does this in CacheFront, a Redis cache in front of its own database that serves more than 40 million reads a second. Each row's last-update time is its version, and a Lua script writes a value only if it's newer.

A version check has a hole of its own, and Meta's post points at it. The check needs the newer version to still be in the cache when the old fill arrives. Replay the stale set with a version check and a writer that deletes. The DEL removes the cache's only record of version 2. A's fill of version 1 finds nothing to compare with, and it's stored. Eviction opens the same hole. When Redis runs out of memory, it throws entries out to make room (Expiry, eviction and memory), and the newer version may go right before the old fill arrives.

Here the shop window picture breaks. A real window would remember a tag it took down a minute ago. Redis remembers nothing about a deleted key, unless you leave something there on purpose.

So keep the version when you drop the value. The writer replaces the entry with a tombstone, {ver: 2} with no name, and gives it a TTL longer than the slowest fill can take, say 10 seconds. Readers treat a tombstone as a miss. A fill of version 1 is refused, because 1 is less than 2. A fill of version 2 replaces the tombstone. Races 3 and 4 of the demo showed both halves: a version check after a plain DEL let the old name in, and the same check after a tombstone refused it.

Every fix so far assumes the writer's delete or tombstone reaches Redis. Next, we'll see what happens when it doesn't.

try.title: A tombstone refuses an old fill, a DEL doesn't
steps: At the redis-cli prompt, clear the key and run the tombstone script: the writer has committed version 2. Read the entry with HGETALL, which prints every field of a hash.
Now two fills arrive: version 1 from a slow reader, then version 2 from a fresh one. Predict both replies before you run them.
The last three lines play Meta's hole: the entry disappears (an eviction, or a writer that only deletes), and the slow reader's version 1 arrives. Predict the HGET.

The tombstone script prints (integer) 1, and HGETALL shows only 1) "ver" and 2) "2": a version with no name. The slow reader's fill of version 1 prints (integer) 0, refused. The fresh fill of version 2 prints (integer) 1, and HGETALL now shows ver 2 and name "Velo Utrecht". Then the hole: DEL prints (integer) 1, the version-1 fill prints (integer) 1, stored, and HGET prints "Fietsen Utrecht". With no version left in the cache, the check had nothing to refuse with.

sections.h: A server that dies before its delete: the database's log, and the TTL as a safety net
sections.html:
A server can die between COMMIT and DEL. The operating system, the program that runs all the others, may stop it for using too much memory, or someone may restart it to install a new version. The commit stands, the delete never runs, and the old copy lives until its TTL ends. This is the other half of the dual-write problem, a partial failure: one change for two systems, and only one of them got it.

The fix is to take the delete away from the program that saved. The database already records every committed change, in commit order, in a log of its own, which it keeps so that it can recover after a crash. PostgreSQL, a popular free database program, calls it the write-ahead log, and MySQL, another one, calls it the binlog. A separate program that reads that log and turns each change into a delete in Redis can't skip a commit, whatever happens to the server that made it. That's change data capture (CDC). Two systems, one truth: dual writes and change data capture builds it properly.

Meta ran it long before the name caught on. On every database machine, a small program called mcsqueal reads MySQL's log of commits, picks out the keys to delete, and sends the deletes to every cache in that part of the world. Only 4% of those deletes find a cached value to remove, which shows how cheap a spare delete is. Uber's CacheFront reads the binlog the same way and keeps Redis within seconds of the database. A binlog holds only committed changes, so data that was never committed never reaches the cache.

Change data capture doesn't end the earlier races. Its deletes arrive a little after the commit, and fills from readers still mix in between them. That's why Uber sends every write into Redis, from either side, through the same version check.

Then measure, because you can't fix a wrong answer you never see. Meta's post "Cache made consistent" describes Polaris, a program that receives the change messages as if it were a cache. A few minutes later, it checks whether the caches still disagree with the database. It reports results in nines: six nines within five minutes means that 99.9999% of cache writes, all but one in a million, agree with the database by then. With the bugs Polaris found, Meta took TAO from six nines to ten.

And keep the TTL. It fixes none of this lesson's races; it only caps how long a wrong copy lives. That cap covers what you haven't found yet, such as a log reader running behind or a bug in your own version check. Uber's default is five minutes for rows that nothing else deletes. Choose yours as in Caching patterns and stampedes, by how long a wrong answer may live.

That's the limit of everything in this lesson. Leases, versions and change data capture make a wrong copy rare and short-lived, never impossible. A cache can be nearly right. Keep the answers that must be right in the database. For a shop's name on a receipt, nearly right is fine. For the flag that suspends a shop, the payment check reads the database.

refs.title: Scaling Memcache at Facebook, section 4.1: regional invalidations

opening:
Picture a bike shop in Utrecht that changes its name. The owner opens the payments app, replaces Fietsen Utrecht with Velo Utrecht and presses Save. An hour later, a customer pays by card, and the receipt still says Fietsen Utrecht.

The new name is in the database. But the app also keeps a copy of each shop's name in Redis, a program that holds data in memory so other programs can read it fast. That copy is the old one.

The code that saved the name deleted the copy right after, as the last lesson taught. It's easy to believe that things happen in the order your code lists them, but on a busy system they don't.

In Caching patterns and stampedes, we put Redis in front of a slow database. In this lesson, we'll replay the race that brought the old name back, and make Redis refuse the old copy in two ways. Then we'll handle a program that crashes before it deletes anything. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a bike shop whose receipts kept its old name for an hour, although every save deleted the copy. A slow reader had put the old name back after the delete. A lease or a version lets Redis refuse that late copy, the database's log makes sure no delete is skipped, and the TTL caps whatever slips through.

Change your display name in an app you use on two devices, and watch the other one. An old name that lingers for minutes is probably a copy waiting out its timer.

Next, we'll use Redis for records that aren't copies at all. How can twenty servers share one count of a card's attempts, and spot a payment that arrives twice?

compare.title: A read that fills only with a live lease, in Java and Kotlin

java.title: LeasedMerchantCache.java
java.html: @Override public String get(String id) { long giveUpAt = System.nanoTime() + patience.toNanos(); while (true) { String cached = redis.get(valueKey(id)); if (cached != null) return cached; // a hit String token = UUID.randomUUID().toString(); if (redis.set(leaseKey(id), token, SetParams.setParams().nx().px(lease.toMillis())) != null) { MerchantTable.Row row = table.read(id); // the lease is ours: load if (row == null) { redis.delex(leaseKey(id), CompareCondition.valueEq(token)); return null; } redis.eval(FILL, List.of(valueKey(id), leaseKey(id)), List.of(token, row.getName(), String.valueOf(TTL_SECONDS))); // refused after a write return row.getName(); } if (System.nanoTime() >= giveUpAt) break; // someone else loads: wait sleep(10); } MerchantTable.Row row = table.read(id); // out of patience: never fill return row == null ? null : row.getName(); }

kotlin.title: LeasedMerchantCache.kt
kotlin.html: override fun get(id: String): String? { val giveUpAt = System.nanoTime() + patience.toNanos() while (true) { redis.get(valueKey(id))?.let { return it } // a hit val token = UUID.randomUUID().toString() if (redis.set(leaseKey(id), token, SetParams.setParams().nx().px(lease.toMillis())) != null) { val row = table.read(id) ?: run { // the lease is ours: load redis.delex(leaseKey(id), CompareCondition.valueEq(token)) return null } redis.eval(FILL, listOf(valueKey(id), leaseKey(id)), listOf(token, row.name, TTL_SECONDS.toString())) // refused after a write return row.name } if (System.nanoTime() >= giveUpAt) break // someone else loads: wait Thread.sleep(10) } return table.read(id)?.name // out of patience: never fill }

compare.note: Both send Redis the same commands: a GET, on a miss one SET ... NX PX for the lease, and one EVAL of the fill script, which refuses the value if a save deleted the lease in the meantime. Kotlin's ?: run { ...; return null } handles a missing row inside the same expression, and table.read(id)?.name folds the last check for a missing row into one line. Java's Thread.sleep can throw InterruptedException, an exception Java makes you handle, so the lab's Java version wraps it in a small sleep helper that marks the thread as interrupted again. Neither version locks anything inside the program: the only thing that keeps two readers apart is the lease in Redis, which is why it works across servers. The lab's real method also runs the beforeFill hook right before the EVAL; it's left out here.

worked.title: A version check with tombstones, in two Lua scripts

steps.say: Start with the record. Each entry is a hash holding the row's version and its name, and readers ask only for the name, with HGET merchant:{m-17} name. A tombstone is the same hash with a version and no name, so it reads as a miss, and nobody needs special code for it.
steps.code:
HSET merchant:{m-17} ver 1 name "Fietsen Utrecht"     # a value: version 1
HGET merchant:{m-17} name                             # "Fietsen Utrecht"
HSET merchant:{m-17} ver 2                            # after DEL: a tombstone for version 2
HGET merchant:{m-17} name                             # (nil): a miss

steps.say: The fill writes only if the cache hasn't seen a newer version. Equal versions are allowed on purpose, so that a fill of version 2 can replace a tombstone of version 2. A fill on an empty key is always stored, which is the hole the tombstone exists to close.
steps.code:
local seen = tonumber(redis.call('HGET', KEYS[1], 'ver'))
if seen and seen > tonumber(ARGV[1]) then return 0 end        -- the cache has seen a newer version
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'ver', ARGV[1], 'name', ARGV[2])
redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], 3600)
return 1

steps.say: The delete replaces the entry with a tombstone of the new version, unless the cache already holds something newer. Its TTL must be longer than the slowest time from read to fill that a reader can take. 10 seconds covers a request that gives up after 5.
steps.code:
local seen = tonumber(redis.call('HGET', KEYS[1], 'ver'))
if seen and seen > tonumber(ARGV[1]) then return 0 end
redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1])
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'ver', ARGV[1])                   -- a version and no name: a tombstone
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[2])                       -- longer than the slowest fill
return 1

steps.say: Call them from the read side and from the save side. The reader passes the version it read along with the row; the writer passes the version it just committed.
steps.code: String get(String id) { String name = redis.hget(key(id), "name"); // a tombstone has no name: a miss if (name != null) return name; MerchantTable.Row row = table.read(id); if (row == null) return null; redis.eval(FILL_IF_NEWER, List.of(key(id)), List.of(String.valueOf(row.getVersion()), row.getName())); return row.getName(); } void afterWrite(String id, long committedVersion) { redis.eval(TOMBSTONE, List.of(key(id)), List.of(String.valueOf(committedVersion), "10000")); }

alt.html: fun get(id: String): String? { redis.hget(key(id), "name")?.let { return it } // a tombstone has no name: a miss val row = table.read(id) ?: return null redis.eval(FILL_IF_NEWER, listOf(key(id)), listOf(row.version.toString(), row.name)) return row.name } fun afterWrite(id: String, committedVersion: Long) { redis.eval(TOMBSTONE, listOf(key(id)), listOf(committedVersion.toString(), "10000")) }

steps.say: Know the hole that's left. A fill slower than the tombstone's 10 seconds finds nothing to compare with and gets in, and so does one that arrives after an eviction removed the tombstone. A version also protects you only if it really names the data next to it. Meta's post describes a fill that read the version and the data at different moments, so the cache held old data under the new version number. Keep the entry's TTL as the cap on all of that.

lab.title: Reproduce the stale set with latches, then close it with a lease
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. All 11 fail: three in StaleSetRaceTest and eight in LeasedMerchantCacheTest, against a Redis that the tests start in Docker. MerchantTable (the database, with a version on each row) and NaiveMerchantCache (the last lesson's cache) are done for you.

In StaleSetRace.kt, write run from its KDoc, the comment above it: two CountDownLatches, reader A on its own thread with a hook that holds it before its fill, and the writer in between. Run ./gradlew :redis:test --tests 'sfz.cache.l07.StaleSetRaceTest'. The first two tests pass: you've made the stepper's timeline happen on purpose, twenty times in a row.
In LeasedMerchantCache.java, write the FILL script, then afterWrite (one DEL of both keys), then get from its javadoc.

Run all 11 tests. a fill whose lease was deleted by a write is refused is the stepper's frame 5 with the fix in place. a reader that misses while another holds the lease waits for that value... is the stampede fix that leases give for free: two misses, one query.
hints: pods.cache { atFill.countDown(); writerDone.await(5, SECONDS) } builds reader A's cache: the lambda (a small function written in place) is its beforeFill hook. The second cache gets pods.cache {}.
The script: if redis.call('GET', KEYS[2]) ~= ARGV[1] then return 0 end, then the SET with 'EX', ARGV[3], then DEL the lease and return 1.
redis.set(leaseKey(id), token, SetParams.setParams().nx().px(lease.toMillis())) returns null when another reader holds the lease.
From Java, a Kotlin property is read through a getter: row.getName().

drill.title: The lease fill from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write the fill script that stores a value only while the caller's lease is still in place. Then write the call from Jedis, the Java library the labs use to talk to Redis, that runs it with a value key, a lease key, a token, a name and a TTL. Last, say which command on the save side makes this script refuse a stale fill.

answer.html: static final String FILL = """ if redis.call('GET', KEYS[2]) ~= ARGV[1] then return 0 end redis.call('SET', KEYS[1], ARGV[2], 'EX', ARGV[3]) redis.call('DEL', KEYS[2]) return 1 """; boolean fill(String valueKey, String leaseKey, String token, String name) { Object r = redis.eval(FILL, List.of(valueKey, leaseKey), List.of(token, name, "3600")); return Long.valueOf(1).equals(r); } // the writer, after its commit: DEL <valueKey> <leaseKey> in one command, which takes the token away

alt.html: val FILL = """ if redis.call('GET', KEYS[2]) ~= ARGV[1] then return 0 end redis.call('SET', KEYS[1], ARGV[2], 'EX', ARGV[3]) redis.call('DEL', KEYS[2]) return 1 """.trimIndent() fun fill(valueKey: String, leaseKey: String, token: String, name: String): Boolean = redis.eval(FILL, listOf(valueKey, leaseKey), listOf(token, name, "3600")) == 1L // the writer, after its commit: DEL <valueKey> <leaseKey> in one command, which takes the token away

recap: A cached value is a copy of one version of a row. The cache stays honest as long as no copy older than the newest delete can get in, and every race in this lesson is a way in.
On a save, delete the copy instead of updating it. Two deletes in any order leave the same empty key, while two servers' updates can arrive out of order.
The stale set: a reader that read before the commit and fills after the delete puts the old value back, for the whole TTL.
A lease (SET ... NX PX on a miss, one DEL of copy and lease on a save, a Lua fill that checks the token) refuses that late fill, and lets only one reader per key load.
A version check refuses fills older than a version the cache has seen, but only while it still holds that version, so leave a tombstone when you delete.

The limit: all of this makes a wrong copy rare and short, never impossible. Take deletes from the database's change log, measure how often the cache is wrong, keep a TTL on every entry, and keep answers that must be right in the database.

explain.prompt: A teammate says: "Our shop cache deletes the key after every commit, so it can't show an old name for more than a few milliseconds." Explain the two ways it still can, and what you would add.
explain.answer: Deleting after the commit is the right rule, and it still leaves two gaps. First, a reader can miss, read the old row, and then stall for a moment, in a garbage-collection pause or a wait for a slow connection. Meanwhile, the writer commits and deletes the key, which is still empty, so the delete does nothing. Then the reader's SET arrives and stores the old row with a full TTL, and nothing will delete it again. Second, the server can crash between its commit and its DEL, and then no delete runs at all. For the first gap, I'd make Redis able to refuse the late fill. One way is a lease: a token taken with SET NX PX on a miss, which the writer's DEL removes and the fill script checks. The other is a version stored with each entry, so a fill older than what the cache has seen is refused, with a tombstone left on delete so the version survives. For the second gap, I'd take the deletes from the database's change log instead of from the server, so a crash can't skip one. And I'd keep a TTL on every entry and measure how often the cache disagrees with the database, because those catch the cases we haven't thought of.

deeper.html:
Where the lease idea comes from. Meta's paper compares leases to a pair of processor instructions, load-link and store-conditional. The first reads a memory address; the second writes it only if nobody wrote the address since the read. A lease does the same for a cache key.

Meta's version bug. "Cache made consistent" walks through a real wrong answer that its tracing found. A rare transaction updated a row's data and its version in two tables. A fill ran in between, and stored the old data with the new version number. The delete then failed with a short-lived error, and the error handler called drop_cache(key, version), which drops an entry only if its version is older than the one given. The cached version wasn't older, so nothing was dropped, and the old data stayed. Thanks to the tracing, the engineer on duty found it in under 30 minutes. The lesson: a version protects you only if it was read at the same moment as the data it labels.

More of memcache's tricks. A new, empty cache cluster that warms itself from a full one could cache a value that the full cluster hadn't deleted yet. Meta's fix: deletes sent to the new cluster carry a two-second hold-off, during which add for that key fails and tells the client to read the database instead. The paper admits that a delete delayed by more than two seconds is still a hole. For writes from a region far from the main database, a "remote marker" key tells later readers to fetch from the main region until the copies catch up. When followers lag: read-your-writes, monotonic reads and consistent prefix, in the Replication track, explains the problem those markers work around.

Caches inside the program have the same races. Redis 6 and later can push deletes to programs that keep copies of keys in their own memory (the Go deeper part of Caching patterns and stampedes). That moves the copy closer to the code, and the stale set can now happen inside one server: a program that reads a key right before a delete and stores it right after. Losing the connection is the other gap. Deletes sent while a program was disconnected never reach it, which is why Jedis empties its local copies whenever a connection drops.

Uber's check. Uber also runs CacheFront in a mode that compares cached rows with the database, and reports 99.99% consistency.

Redis 8.4's compare-and-set. SET key value IFEQ <expected> writes only if the current value equals <expected>, and DELEX key IFEQ <expected> deletes only then. They help when the value itself carries the token or version. When the check must look at another key, as the lease fill does, or compare numbers, as the version check does, a Lua script is still the tool.

For the general argument, from dual writes to building every system from one ordered log, read Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 12, "Keeping Systems in Sync".
